modules.title: 1 · The DiD idea
modules.summary: Why comparing one group's before/after change against a control group's change isolates a causal effect.

stages.title: Two comparisons are better than one
stages.html:
The problem DiD solves

Suppose a state raises its minimum wage and we want the effect on employment. Two naive strategies both fail:

  • Before vs. after in the treated state alone: employment also moves because of the economy, seasons, trends — not just the policy.
  • Treated vs. control at one point in time: the two states differ for many baseline reasons (industry mix, demographics) that have nothing to do with the policy.

Each single comparison is contaminated. Difference-in-Differences (DiD) combines them: take the change in the treated group and subtract the change in a control group over the same window.

Key idea. The control group's change estimates what would have happened to the treated group anyway. Subtracting it strips out common trends and common shocks, leaving the causal effect.

Four cells

DiD lives on a 2×2 grid: {treated, control} × {before, after}. We need the average outcome in each of the four cells.

stages.title: The estimator in words and symbols
stages.html:
Differencing twice

Let ȳ denote a group-period average outcome. The treated group's raw change over time is:

Δtreated = ȳ(treated, after) − ȳ(treated, before)

But part of that is just the trend everyone experienced. The control group reveals that trend:

Δcontrol = ȳ(control, after) − ȳ(control, before)

The DiD estimate is the difference of these differences:

ATT̂ = Δtreated − Δcontrol

This number estimates the Average Treatment effect on the Treated (ATT) — how much the policy changed outcomes for the units that actually got it.

Key idea. The control group is a counterfactual machine: it tells us the change the treated group would have had with no treatment. The leftover is the effect.

stages.title: Compute DiD from four cell means
stages.note: Simulate a treated and a control group, before and after. True effect (ATT) is 4. We recover it by hand from the four averages.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
treated = rng.integers(0, 2, n)        # 1 = treated group, 0 = control
post    = rng.integers(0, 2, n)        # 1 = after, 0 = before
ATT = 4.0
# baseline gap 3 (treated higher), common time trend 2, true effect 4 only when treated & post
y = 10 + 3*treated + 2*post + ATT*treated*post + rng.normal(0, 2, n)
df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, treated=treated, post=post))

cell = df.groupby(['treated','post'])['y'].mean().unstack()
print('Cell means (rows=treated, cols=post):')
print(cell.round(3))

d_treated = cell.loc[1,1] - cell.loc[1,0]
d_control = cell.loc[0,1] - cell.loc[0,0]
did = d_treated - d_control
print(f'\nchange in treated group : {d_treated:.3f}')
print(f'change in control group: {d_control:.3f}')
print(f'DiD estimate (ATT)     : {did:.3f}   (true = {ATT})')

stages.title: See the four cells move
stages.note: Slide the true ATT and the common time trend. The DiD estimate should track the ATT and ignore the trend.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600
treated = rng.integers(0,2,n); post = rng.integers(0,2,n)
y = 10 + 3*treated + {{trend}}*post + {{att}}*treated*post + rng.normal(0,2,n)
df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, treated=treated, post=post))
c = df.groupby(['treated','post'])['y'].mean().unstack()
did = (c.loc[1,1]-c.loc[1,0]) - (c.loc[0,1]-c.loc[0,0])
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot([0,1],[c.loc[1,0],c.loc[1,1]],'o-',color='#da9100',lw=2,label='treated')
plt.plot([0,1],[c.loc[0,0],c.loc[0,1]],'o-',color='#c9c6ac',lw=2,label='control')
# counterfactual: treated baseline + control's change
cf = c.loc[1,0] + (c.loc[0,1]-c.loc[0,0])
plt.plot([0,1],[c.loc[1,0],cf],'--',color='#af983f',lw=2,label='treated counterfactual')
plt.xticks([0,1],['before','after']); plt.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.title(f'DiD (ATT) estimate = {did:.2f}')

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: A common economy-wide shock makes BOTH groups' outcomes rise by 5 between before and after. What happens to the DiD estimate?
choices: It rises by 5
It rises by 10
It is unchanged
It falls by 5
stages.hint: DiD subtracts the control group's change, which now contains that +5.
stages.explain: A shock common to both groups enters both Δtreated and Δcontrol, so it cancels in the difference of differences. DiD is designed to be immune to such common shocks.

stages.title: The control group is a what?
stages.prompt: In DiD, the control group's before-to-after change is used as an estimate of the treated group's ___ change — what would have happened to the treated units absent treatment.
stages.lead: You just saw that subtracting the control group's change strips out common trends and shocks, leaving the causal effect.
stages.hint: It is the change the treated group *would* have had with no policy — a word starting with 'counter'.
stages.explain: The 'control is just another treated group' slip. The control group is a counterfactual machine: its change estimates the trend/shocks the treated group would also have felt, so subtracting it nets those out and leaves the treatment effect. The tempting reading — that the control is simply a second observation of the effect — fails because the control is never treated; its only job is to reveal the common trend. This holds only if that common trend really is shared (parallel trends); if the groups' trends diverge, the control is the wrong counterfactual.

modules.title: 2 · The 2×2 estimator
modules.summary: The DiD estimate is exactly the interaction coefficient in a regression of y on treated, post, and their product.

stages.title: DiD is one regression coefficient
stages.html:
From four means to a regression

Computing four cell means and differencing is intuitive, but a single regression gives the same number plus a standard error, a t-statistic, and the ability to add controls. We regress the outcome on two dummies and their interaction:

y = β₀ + β₁·treated + β₂·post + β₃·(treated·post) + ε

Read each coefficient off the 2×2 grid:

  • β₀ = control group, before (the baseline cell).
  • β₁ = treated-vs-control gap before treatment (a level difference).
  • β₂ = before-vs-after change in the control group (the common trend).
  • β₃ = the extra change in the treated group on top of the trend — this is the DiD / ATT.
Key idea. The interaction term treated:post is the difference-in-differences. Its coefficient β₃ is the ATT, and its standard error gives you inference for free.

stages.title: Why the interaction equals the double difference
stages.html:
Plug in the four cells

Evaluate the regression equation at each cell (ignoring ε, which averages to zero):

  • control, before: ŷ = β₀
  • control, after: ŷ = β₀ + β₂
  • treated, before: ŷ = β₀ + β₁
  • treated, after: ŷ = β₀ + β₁ + β₂ + β₃

Now form the double difference:

(treated,after − treated,before) − (control,after − control,before)

= (β₂ + β₃) − (β₂) = β₃

Everything except β₃ cancels. The regression is algebraically identical to the hand calculation — but it scales to many covariates and clustered standard errors.

Key idea. smf.ols("y ~ treated*post", df) in statsmodels automatically adds treated, post, and treated:post. Just read off params['treated:post'].

stages.title: Estimate the ATT with statsmodels
stages.note: Same simulated data as Module 1. The interaction coefficient matches the hand-computed DiD exactly, and now we get a standard error and p-value.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
treated = rng.integers(0,2,n); post = rng.integers(0,2,n)
ATT = 4.0
y = 10 + 3*treated + 2*post + ATT*treated*post + rng.normal(0,2,n)
df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, treated=treated, post=post))

res = smf.ols('y ~ treated*post', df).fit()
print(res.summary().tables[1])
print()
print(f"ATT (treated:post) = {res.params['treated:post']:.3f}")
print(f"std error          = {res.bse['treated:post']:.3f}")
print(f"true ATT           = {ATT}")

stages.title: Noise vs. precision of the ATT
stages.note: Crank up the idiosyncratic noise σ and watch the point estimate stay roughly right while its standard error balloons.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600
treated = rng.integers(0,2,n); post = rng.integers(0,2,n)
y = 10 + 3*treated + 2*post + {{att}}*treated*post + rng.normal(0,{{noise}},n)
df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, treated=treated, post=post))
res = smf.ols('y ~ treated*post', df).fit()
b = res.params['treated:post']; se = res.bse['treated:post']
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.axhline({{att}}, color='#6f6b57', ls='--', lw=1.5, label='true ATT')
plt.errorbar([0], [b], yerr=[1.96*se], fmt='o', color='#da9100', ecolor='#c9c6ac', capsize=6, ms=9, label='estimate +/- 95% CI')
plt.xlim(-1,1); plt.xticks([]); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'ATT_hat = {b:.2f}   SE = {se:.3f}')

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: In the regression y ~ treated*post, which coefficient is the causal DiD estimate (the ATT)?
choices: The coefficient on 'treated'
The coefficient on 'post'
The coefficient on 'treated:post'
The intercept
stages.hint: Which coefficient survives the double difference after the others cancel?
stages.explain: Only the interaction 'treated:post' captures the extra change in the treated group beyond the common trend; the other terms cancel in the difference-of-differences.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: What does the coefficient on 'treated' (β₁) by itself represent?
choices: The treatment effect
The pre-treatment level gap between treated and control groups
The common time trend
The post-period outcome of the control group
stages.hint: Set post = 0 and compare treated to control.
stages.explain: β₁ is the baseline (before-period) difference in levels between the groups. It is a fixed gap, not an effect — DiD explicitly allows the groups to differ in levels.

stages.title: Equal pre-treatment levels?
stages.prompt: DiD requires the treated and control groups to have equal outcome levels before treatment.
stages.hint: Which coefficient in y ~ treated*post absorbs a fixed before-period gap between the groups?
stages.explain: The levels-vs-trends confusion. DiD allows any baseline level gap — that gap is exactly what β₁ (the 'treated' coefficient) absorbs, which is why the module called it a fixed level difference, not an effect. The tempting belief — that the groups must start equal — confuses a constant level gap (harmless, differenced away) with a difference in trends (fatal). Boundary: different starting levels are fine; differently-sloped trends break identification. Pivot word: levels (ok) vs trends (not ok).

modules.title: 3 · Parallel trends
modules.summary: DiD is valid only if the groups would have moved in parallel absent treatment; a pre-trend difference biases the ATT.

stages.title: The one assumption that matters
stages.html:
Parallel trends

DiD does not require the two groups to be identical — they can sit at different levels (that is β₁). What it does require is that, in the absence of treatment, the treated and control groups would have followed parallel paths over time.

E[y(after) − y(before) | treated, no treatment] = E[y(after) − y(before) | control]

If this holds, the control group's change is exactly the counterfactual change for the treated group, and β₃ recovers the true ATT. If it fails, the control group's trend is the wrong counterfactual and the estimate is biased.

Key idea. Parallel trends is about the slopes (changes), not the levels. Different starting points are fine; differently-shaped trajectories are fatal.

stages.title: What a violation does to the estimate
stages.html:
Trend contamination

Suppose the treated group was already growing faster than the control group before any treatment — say by δ per period (a differential pre-trend). Then even with zero true effect, the treated group's change exceeds the control's change purely from the divergent trend.

The DiD estimator cannot tell that divergence apart from a treatment effect, so it reports:

ATT̂ ≈ true ATT + (differential trend over the window)

A positive pre-trend inflates the estimate; a negative one deflates it. This is why a credible DiD study spends most of its effort defending parallel trends, typically by showing the groups moved together in the periods before treatment.

Key idea. Parallel trends is untestable for the post period (we never observe the treated counterfactual). The standard evidence is indirect: equal trends in the pre-period make a parallel post-period plausible.

stages.title: Inject a pre-trend and watch the bias
stages.note: True ATT is 4, but the treated group also drifts upward 1.5 per period faster than control. The naive 2×2 DiD over-states the effect.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
treated = rng.integers(0,2,n); post = rng.integers(0,2,n)
ATT = 4.0
bias_per_period = 1.5   # treated grows faster regardless of treatment -> violates parallel trends
# 'post' adds one period of the differential trend on top of the true effect
y = (10 + 3*treated + 2*post
     + bias_per_period*treated*post   # the offending differential trend
     + ATT*treated*post               # the real effect
     + rng.normal(0,2,n))
df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, treated=treated, post=post))
res = smf.ols('y ~ treated*post', df).fit()
est = res.params['treated:post']
print(f'true ATT                 : {ATT}')
print(f'differential trend (bias): {bias_per_period}')
print(f'DiD estimate             : {est:.3f}')
print(f'bias                     : {est - ATT:+.3f}  (should be ~ +{bias_per_period})')

stages.title: Dial the pre-trend violation
stages.note: Set the true ATT and a differential trend that breaks parallelism. The dashed line is what the treated group WOULD do under parallel trends; the gap to the orange observed line is the bias the estimator absorbs.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
treated = rng.integers(0,2,n); post = rng.integers(0,2,n)
y = (10 + 3*treated + 2*post + {{violate}}*treated*post + {{att}}*treated*post + rng.normal(0,2,n))
df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, treated=treated, post=post))
res = smf.ols('y ~ treated*post', df).fit()
est = res.params['treated:post']
c = df.groupby(['treated','post'])['y'].mean().unstack()
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot([0,1],[c.loc[1,0],c.loc[1,1]],'o-',color='#da9100',lw=2,label='treated (observed)')
plt.plot([0,1],[c.loc[0,0],c.loc[0,1]],'o-',color='#c9c6ac',lw=2,label='control')
cf = c.loc[1,0] + (c.loc[0,1]-c.loc[0,0])
plt.plot([0,1],[c.loc[1,0],cf],'--',color='#af983f',lw=2,label='parallel-trends counterfactual')
plt.xticks([0,1],['before','after']); plt.legend(fontsize=7)
plt.title(f'ATT_hat = {est:.2f}  (true {{att}}, bias {est-{{att}}:+.2f})')

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: The treated group sits 8 points above the control group in BOTH the before and after periods, and both rise by 3 over time. Is parallel trends satisfied?
choices: No, the 8-point gap violates it
Yes, the gap is constant so the trends are parallel
Cannot tell without the true ATT
No, because they are not at the same level
stages.hint: Parallel trends concerns changes over time, not the level gap.
stages.explain: A constant level gap with equal changes (both +3) means the trends are parallel. DiD allows different levels; it only needs equal trends.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: If the treated group was already trending up faster than control before treatment, the standard 2×2 DiD estimate of a positive ATT will tend to be:
choices: Unbiased
Biased upward (too large)
Biased downward (too small)
Exactly zero
stages.hint: The estimator mistakes the extra pre-existing growth for treatment effect.
stages.explain: A positive differential pre-trend adds to the treated group's change, and DiD attributes that extra change to treatment, overstating the ATT.

stages.title: Big post gap, diverging pre-trends
stages.prompt: If the treated and control groups had different pre-treatment trends, the DiD estimate is still unbiased as long as the post-period gap is large.
stages.hint: What does the module say the estimate equals when there is a differential trend δ per period?
stages.explain: The parallel-trends-is-everything trap. Identification rests entirely on parallel counterfactual trends; diverging pre-trends are direct evidence that assumption fails, and the module showed the estimate becomes ATT̂ ≈ true ATT + (differential trend over the window). A large post gap is no defense — the seductive belief that a big effect 'swamps' the bias fails because the trend difference is baked into that gap and DiD cannot separate the two. Boundary: only when pre-trends are parallel does the control's change equal the treated counterfactual and β₃ recover the true ATT.

stages.title: DiD from a 2×2 table
stages.prompt: A 2×2 DiD: the treated group's mean goes 40 → 62, the control group's mean goes 38 → 45. Enter the DiD estimate (treated change minus control change), in points.
stages.hint: First find each group's change, then subtract: (62−40) − (45−38).
stages.explain: The 'forget the counterfactual trend' trap. (62−40) − (45−38) = 22 − 7 = 15. The control's change of 7 is the common shock the treated group would also have felt, so subtracting it nets out the trend. The seductive wrong answer is 22 — the raw treated change — which credits the policy with the entire before/after move and ignores that part of it was just the shared trend. Boundary: 22 would be the right answer only if the control's change were 0, i.e. nothing happened to anyone absent treatment.

modules.title: 4 · Event-study / dynamic DiD
modules.summary: Estimate a separate effect for each period relative to treatment to test pre-trends and trace the effect's dynamics.

stages.title: From one number to a whole path
stages.html:
The event-study design

The 2×2 estimator collapses everything into a single before/after contrast. With a panel of many periods we can do better: estimate a separate treated-vs-control gap for every period, relative to a chosen baseline period (usually the last period before treatment).

We interact the treated dummy with a full set of time dummies. Picking period r as the reference, the coefficient on treatedₜ is:

θₜ = (treated − control gap in period t) − (treated − control gap in period r)

Plotting θₜ against t gives the event-study plot, the single most important diagnostic in modern DiD.

Key idea. Pre-treatment coefficients (t < treatment) should be near zero — that is your visual test of parallel trends. Post-treatment coefficients trace how the effect turns on and evolves.

stages.title: Reading leads and lags
stages.html:
Leads, lags, and the reference period

  • Leads (periods before treatment, t < T*): these are a falsification test. If parallel trends holds, the treated and control groups tracked each other beforehand, so the leads should hug zero. Leads that drift away from zero signal a pre-trend and undercut the design.
  • Reference period (t = T*−1): normalized to exactly 0 by construction. Every other coefficient is measured relative to it, so it has no error bar.
  • Lags (periods at/after treatment): the dynamic treatment effects. They might jump immediately, ramp up gradually, or fade out.

In statsmodels we use a panel and the formula y ~ C(time, Treatment(reference=r))*treated + C(unit), then read off the coefficients named ...:treated. The C(unit) term adds unit fixed effects, absorbing every time-invariant difference between units. (The standalone treated term is then collinear with the unit dummies and contributes nothing extra — the per-period interactions carry the identification.)

Key idea. Flat pre-period coefficients are necessary, not sufficient — but a clean event-study plot with near-zero leads is the strongest practical evidence a DiD can offer.

stages.title: Build a panel and run an event study
stages.note: Multi-period panel: treatment turns on at time 4 with true effect 3. We estimate per-period effects and plot leads & lags with 95% intervals. Pre-period coefficients should sit near zero.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, nunit, treat_time, ref = 8, 60, 4, 3
rows = []
for u in range(nunit):
    g = 1 if u < nunit//2 else 0        # first half treated
    ai = rng.normal(0, 1)               # unit fixed effect
    for t in range(T):
        eff = 3.0 if (g == 1 and t >= treat_time) else 0.0
        y = 5 + ai + 0.5*t + eff + rng.normal(0, 1)
        rows.append((u, t, g, y))
df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['unit','time','treated','y'])

res = smf.ols(f'y ~ C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))*treated + C(unit)', df).fit()
ts, est, se = [], [], []
for t in range(T):
    ts.append(t)
    if t == ref:
        est.append(0.0); se.append(0.0); continue
    k = f'C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))[T.{t}]:treated'
    est.append(res.params[k]); se.append(res.bse[k])

for t,e in zip(ts,est): print(f'period {t}: effect = {e:+.3f}')
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.errorbar(ts, est, yerr=[1.96*s for s in se], fmt='o-', color='#da9100', ecolor='#c9c6ac', capsize=3)
plt.axhline(0, color='#6f6b57', lw=1)
plt.axvline(treat_time-0.5, color='#af983f', ls='--', label='treatment starts')
plt.xlabel('period'); plt.ylabel('treated - control gap'); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title('Event study: leads near 0, lags near +3')

stages.title: Pre-trend vs. true effect in the event-study plot
stages.note: Add a true post-treatment ATT and a per-period pre-trend that breaks parallelism. Watch the LEADS lift off zero when you introduce a pre-trend — exactly the warning sign analysts look for.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, pandas as pd, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
T, nunit, treat_time, ref = 8, 60, 4, 3
rows = []
for u in range(nunit):
    g = 1 if u < nunit//2 else 0
    ai = rng.normal(0,1)
    for t in range(T):
        eff = {{att}} if (g==1 and t>=treat_time) else 0.0
        trend = {{pretrend}}*t*g          # divergence in every period -> shows up in leads too
        y = 5 + ai + 0.5*t + trend + eff + rng.normal(0,1)
        rows.append((u,t,g,y))
df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=['unit','time','treated','y'])
res = smf.ols(f'y ~ C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))*treated + C(unit)', df).fit()
ts, est, se = [], [], []
for t in range(T):
    ts.append(t)
    if t == ref:
        est.append(0.0); se.append(0.0); continue
    k = f'C(time, Treatment(reference={ref}))[T.{t}]:treated'
    est.append(res.params[k]); se.append(res.bse[k])
pre = [est[t] for t in range(treat_time)]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.errorbar(ts, est, yerr=[1.96*s for s in se], fmt='o-', color='#da9100', ecolor='#c9c6ac', capsize=3)
plt.axhline(0, color='#6f6b57', lw=1)
plt.axvline(treat_time-0.5, color='#af983f', ls='--', label='treatment starts')
plt.xlabel('period'); plt.ylabel('treated - control gap'); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'max |lead| = {max(abs(p) for p in pre):.2f}  (should be ~0 if valid)')

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: In an event-study plot, what is the purpose of inspecting the PRE-treatment (lead) coefficients?
choices: They measure the treatment effect
They test the parallel-trends assumption — they should be near zero
They set the reference period
They measure how fast the effect fades out
stages.hint: Before treatment there can be no effect, so any nonzero value means something else is going on.
stages.explain: Leads capture treated-vs-control differences before treatment, where the effect must be zero. Near-zero leads support parallel trends; nonzero leads reveal a pre-trend that invalidates the design.

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Why is the reference period's coefficient exactly 0 with no confidence interval?
choices: The effect happens to be zero there
Every other period is measured relative to it, so it is normalized to 0 by construction
Its standard error is too large to plot
Treatment has no effect in that period
stages.hint: All θₜ are differences relative to that one omitted period.
stages.explain: The reference (omitted) period is the baseline against which all other coefficients are defined, so it is mechanically 0 and carries no sampling uncertainty.

stages.title: Reading a significant lead
stages.prompt: Your event-study plot shows a pre-treatment (lead) coefficient that is large and statistically significant, well away from zero. What does this tell you?
choices: It is reassuring — a significant pre-period coefficient confirms the design is working
It is a warning — a nonzero lead signals a pre-trend that undercuts parallel trends
It measures how quickly the treatment effect fades after treatment
It sets the reference period, so it should be large by construction
why: Backwards: leads should hug zero. A significant lead is evidence AGAINST parallel trends, not for the design.
Leads are before treatment, where the effect is zero by definition — they cannot measure post-treatment dynamics.
The reference period is the one normalized to 0 with no error bar; it is not the lead you are reading.
stages.hint: Where the effect must be zero, a coefficient far from zero is bad news, not good.
stages.explain: The 'significant pre-trend is reassuring' trap. Leads sit before treatment, where the true effect is zero, so they should hug zero; a large significant lead is evidence the groups were already diverging — a pre-trend that invalidates the design. The tempting belief flips the logic of a falsification test: you want to fail to reject here, not to find significance. Boundary: flat (near-zero) leads are necessary but not sufficient — failing to reject a pre-trend makes parallelism plausible, it never proves the untestable post-period counterfactual.

stages.title: What the event-study plot tells you
stages.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about an event-study (dynamic DiD) plot are TRUE?
choices: Pre-treatment (lead) coefficients should be near zero if parallel trends holds
The reference period's coefficient is exactly 0 by construction, with no confidence interval
Post-treatment (lag) coefficients trace how the effect turns on and evolves over time
Flat pre-period leads prove the parallel-trends assumption holds in the post period
A statistically significant lead coefficient is reassuring evidence for the design
stages.hint: Two of the five are classic traps: one over-claims what flat leads prove, one misreads what a significant lead means.
stages.explain: The 'flat leads = proven parallelism' over-claim. True: leads near zero are the visual test of parallel trends; the reference period is mechanically 0 with no error bar; lags trace the dynamic effect. False trap 1 — flat pre-period leads are necessary but not sufficient: parallel trends in the post period is untestable, since the treated counterfactual is never observed, so leads make it plausible, not proven. False trap 2 — a significant lead is the opposite of reassuring; it signals a pre-trend. Boundary: the event-study only ever offers indirect, pre-period evidence — it can falsify the design but never certify the post-period counterfactual.
